chapters.title: 8.1 Writing Custom Commands
chapters.overviewText: Cypress.Commands.add registers parent (fresh chain), child ({ prevSubject: true }), or dual ({ prevSubject: 'optional' }) commands in support/commands.js. A child command that should continue the chain must return subject — omitting it is the most common first-time bug. Prefer options objects over positional args. Don't extract a two-line sequence used once; threshold is roughly 3+ identical sites or a name that reads clearly (cy.loginAs).
chapters.why: Every earlier cy.loginAs / getByCy / interceptLeaveApi forward-reference lands here. Miscategorizing prevSubject and dropping the subject are the bugs that make custom commands feel 'broken.' Playwright's equivalent is often a plain async function plus fixtures for lifecycle.
chapters.when: When the same login, data-cy getter, or leave-submit sequence appears across specs, and when wrapping ajv as validateSchema (Part 6.2).

practical.scenario: You want cy.getByCy('submit'), cy.submitLeaveRequest({ type, start, end }), and a child .shouldBeApproved() on a leave row.
practical.pass: You add parent getByCy, parent submitLeaveRequest with an options object, child shouldBeApproved that returns subject, and a Chainable .d.ts entry.
practical.fail: You forget return subject, use five positional args, or wrap a one-spec two-liner as a global command.

chapters.customSummary:
- Arrives late in the manual deliberately — every prior forward-reference (loginAs, getByCy, interceptLeaveApi, fillForm) is this chapter's payoff; premature abstraction before feeling real repetition tends to produce commands that fight you later
- Cypress.Commands.add(name, [options], fn), registered once via support/commands.js → imported by support/e2e.js, available in every spec automatically
- Three types, same as built-ins: parent (starts fresh, ignores prior subject), child ({ prevSubject: true }, errors without a subject), dual ({ prevSubject: 'optional' }, works either way — branch on whether subject is undefined). { prevSubject: ['element'] } further restricts the accepted subject type. Miscategorizing produces a specific, genuinely informative error
- The passthrough convention: a child command meant to continue the chain must explicitly return subject — omitting it breaks the next command in the chain with an undefined subject, the most common first-time bug (directly parallels Part 2.3's .then() passthrough rule)
- Terminal commands (no return value) are fine when chaining further genuinely isn't meaningful (resetAndSeedData)
- A command's body enqueues as many internal cy.* calls as needed — collapses to one line in the Command Log summary but expands on demand, keeping a test's top-level narrative readable
- Prefer an options-object argument over positional args for anything likely to grow — new optional fields don't break existing call sites
- Cypress.Commands.overwrite() modifies a built-in's implementation (receives originalFn first, call it) — belongs to 8.2, not this chapter, but the API lives here
- Assertion-style custom commands should delegate to a real .should() internally to inherit genuine retry behavior, not fake it with a one-shot check (mirrors Part 6.2's validateSchema pattern)
- Not every repeated block deserves a command — the real cost is an added indirection layer in the Command Log exactly when a failure needs clarity. Rough threshold: 3+ genuinely identical use sites, or one use site whose named intent reads meaningfully better than its inlined steps
- TypeScript: every custom command needs a matching .d.ts Chainable entry (Part 1.8) — untyped commands lose autocomplete and typo protection, undermining a chunk of TS's value for the suite
- vs Playwright: no registration mechanism needed at all for simple cases — reusable logic is just a plain async function, since test code has no command-queue constraint to work around. For structured, lifecycle-aware reuse, Playwright reaches for its fixture system (test.extend) — categorically more powerful (handles teardown, composable dependencies) than Cypress commands, which have no built-in teardown concept at all. vs Selenium: no mechanism either — just a function/method/Page Object method in the host language, same simplicity as Playwright's plain-function case but without either tool's chaining integration

chapters.title: 8.2 Overwriting Existing Commands
chapters.overviewText: Cypress.Commands.overwrite wraps a built-in: the callback always receives originalFn first and should call it. Additive .add() cannot break old call sites; overwrite changes every call in the suite, including plugins. Prefer a named cy.visitAndLog over overwriting visit. Never casually overwrite .should() — a wrapper bug becomes a suite-wide outage. Check for a config option (scrollBehavior) before overwriting click.
chapters.why: Overwrite has the widest blast radius in this Part. Interviewers want you to name originalFn, the plugin risk, and the safer .add() alternative.
chapters.when: When adding CI visit logging, guarding cy.type() against non-strings, or fixing sticky-header click failures — after checking config first.

practical.scenario: CI-only failures need a visit trace; sticky header covers buttons; someone proposes wrapping .should() to log every assertion.
practical.pass: You overwrite visit to cy.task('log') then originalFn, set scrollBehavior: 'center' in config instead of overwriting click, and reject the .should() wrapper.
practical.fail: You overwrite .should() with cy.log, or reimplement type() from scratch without calling originalFn.

chapters.customSummary:
- Categorically riskier than .add(): adding is purely additive; overwriting changes behavior retroactively for every existing call site in the whole codebase, including third-party plugins you didn't write
- Signature always receives originalFn first — you're wrapping, not blindly replacing; almost always call it rather than reimplementing from scratch
- Legitimate uses: project-wide debugging instrumentation (log every cy.visit() — genuinely useful for CI-only failures, Part 12.1); enforcing a team convention as an immediate, clear error (typed-check .type()'s input); adjusting a genuinely poor-fit default — though check for a plain config option first (e.g. scrollBehavior: 'center' globally is usually a better fix than overwriting .click())
- The concrete danger: overwriting a foundational command like .should() means a bug in the wrapper — even a typo, even an unexpected internal-call shape — can break every assertion in the entire suite simultaneously, a suite-wide outage rather than a contained failure. Also a real, if smaller, performance cost when added to a command that fires constantly
- Safer default alternative: a new, differently-named .add() command instead of overwriting — more work to adopt (call sites must opt in explicitly) but bounds any bug's blast radius to exactly the tests deliberately updated to use it
- vs Playwright: no direct equivalent — no global command registry to rewrap, since actions are plain function calls. Closest analogue is wrapping/extending the page object via a custom fixture: more code, but more explicit about what's changing, which partly mitigates the "invisible global behavior change" risk. vs Selenium: no equivalent either — would require subclassing/monkey-patching WebElement/WebDriver directly, rare in real codebases

chapters.title: 8.3 Support Files
chapters.overviewText: commands.js is vocabulary (custom commands). e2e.js is operating policy before every test: import commands, plugins, uncaught:exception allowlist, dialog defaults, universal beforeEach. Split commands/ by concern once you pass ~15–20 commands. component.js is a parallel file for CT. supportFile: false is almost never right on a real project. A support-file beforeEach has no per-spec opt-out.
chapters.why: A mature e2e.js is the encoded policy of the whole suite. Putting feature-specific hooks there makes failing tests undiscoverable six months later.
chapters.when: Scaffolding support after Part 1, adding axe/grep/real-events, or when commands.js hits a few hundred lines.

practical.scenario: Global analytics noise, ResizeObserver exceptions, loginAs/getByCy/seedEmployee, and a React component-testing setup.
practical.pass: You keep e2e.js policy-only, split commands/{auth,selectors,api,forms,assertions}.js, reuse getByCy from component.js, and leave loginAs out of CT support.
practical.fail: You put leave-approvals beforeEach in e2e.js, or set supportFile: false because 'less magic.'

chapters.customSummary:
- Both auto-load before every spec (Part 1.3), but answer different questions: commands.js = "what new vocabulary do I want?" (8.1/8.2's definitions) vs e2e.js = "what must happen before literally every test, regardless of subject?"
- A mature e2e.js is the accumulated operating policy of the whole manual's global concerns in one place: command import, third-party plugin registration (Testing Library, cypress-real-events, cypress-axe, @cypress/grep), the filtered uncaught:exception handler (Part 3.14), global dialog defaults (Part 3.9), global window:before:load hooks, and a genuinely universal beforeEach (e.g., silencing analytics noise)
- commands.js should be split by concern into a commands/ folder (auth.js, selectors.js, api.js, forms.js, assertions.js) once it passes roughly 15–20 commands, all re-imported from the top-level commands.js — keeps a growing support layer navigable and maps onto team ownership boundaries
- support/component.js is a separate, parallel file for Component Testing (Part 9.5) — genuinely different setup needs (framework mount config, no full-app auth/visit hooks). Commands genuinely shared by both testing types can live in one shared file imported by both
- supportFile: false disables the whole mechanism — essentially never appropriate for a real project; the only defensible case is a minimal maintainer-facing bug-reproduction repo
- Scope discipline: a beforeEach in e2e.js runs before every test in the entire run with no opt-out short of restructuring it — reserve the support file for genuinely universal concerns; anything feature-specific belongs in that feature's own spec file, where a future reader can actually find it
- vs Playwright: nearest equivalents are global-setup/global-teardown (run once for the whole run, not per-test — a meaningfully different lifecycle than e2e.js's per-test beforeEach) plus { auto: true } base fixtures via test.extend() for genuinely per-test universal setup — same effect, expressed through the fixture/DI system rather than one conventional file. vs Selenium: no equivalent convention at all — whatever the host test framework offers (JUnit shared base class, pytest conftest.py autouse fixtures)

chapters.title: 8.4 Page Object Model vs App Actions
chapters.overviewText: Cypress docs recommend against POM because fluent return-this chaining implies synchronous execution the command queue does not have — bugs then hide one layer down around retry-ability and aliases. App Actions model actions, not pages: custom commands that use API/state for setup and UI only for the thing under test (Part 6.3 packaged as a library). Playwright officially recommends POM because awaits are real. Group commands by feature without classes.
chapters.why: Selenium-background engineers reach for POM by instinct. Explaining why it's wrong for Cypress specifically (command queue, not 'POM is bad') is a senior signal. App Actions is the organizational form of shortcut-what-isn't-under-test.
chapters.when: When structuring the HRM suite's reusable layer, reviewing a LeaveApprovalsPage class, or answering 'do you use page objects in Cypress?' in interviews.

practical.pass: You replace it with cy.createLeaveRequest() (API) + cy.approveLeaveRequestViaUi(name), selectors still visible, maybe a non-fluent payrollGrid.cell() helper for the grid.
practical.fail: You keep return-this chaining, hide every data-cy behind getRows(), or say 'POM is always wrong' without naming the queue.

chapters.customSummary:
- Cypress's official docs explicitly recommend against POM — worth understanding why, not just complying
- The mismatch traces to Part 2.3's command queue: Selenium's blocking, synchronous calls make fluent return this chaining (.visit().approveFirst()) an accurate representation of execution order. In Cypress, every cy.* call inside a POM method is enqueued, not executed — chaining doesn't error, but it wraps a fundamentally async, queued model in an interface that implies synchronous execution, and this mismatch surfaces specifically around retry-ability and aliasing, one abstraction layer removed from visibility
- Second friction: POM hides selectors as private class implementation detail behind method names, working against Part 4's whole discipline that data-cy selectors should make test intent directly legible — wrapping them in getRows() three files away adds a lookup step exactly when a failing test needs clarity
- App Actions is Cypress's own recommended alternative — not a new philosophy, but the organizational packaging of Part 6.3's "shortcut what isn't under test, use the UI for what is" discipline: model actions, not pages, as flat custom commands (8.1) that internally pick API/state manipulation for setup and real UI interaction for the thing actually under test
- App Actions avoids POM's specific problems: no return this masking the queue (each action is an independent, real chainable, like any built-in); selectors stay visible and close to the test's concern rather than buried in a class; composes naturally with aliases, cy.session(), and fixtures because it's just ordinary custom commands, not a competing abstraction
- A defensible middle ground: group action commands by feature area in files (mirrors 8.3's commands/ split) without wrapping them in classes or fluent chaining — gets POM's discoverability benefit with none of its command-queue friction
- A narrow case where a thin object is still reasonable: grouping selectors (not fluent, stateful actions) for a genuinely complex, highly-stateful page (a grid, a kanban board) — legitimate as long as it doesn't reintroduce chained pseudo-synchronous methods or store command results across method boundaries. The real dividing line is "does this abstraction pretend commands execute synchronously," not "is it a class"
- vs Playwright: the opposite official recommendation — POM is actively encouraged, and for good architectural reason: Playwright's commands genuinely are await-able, so fluent POM chaining accurately represents real execution order rather than hiding a queue underneath it. The core takeaway: a pattern's fitness depends on the execution model beneath it, not on abstract merit — POM isn't wrong, it's wrong for Cypress specifically, traceable directly back to Part 2.3. vs Selenium: POM's native, original habitat — designed for exactly Selenium's synchronous blocking call model, which is precisely why Selenium-background engineers reach for it in Cypress by instinct, and precisely why that instinct is worth deliberately unlearning
